## Round 459 (#459) -- the CPU brought the timer and the board brought the clock, and nothing checked that the two agreed

`dev_sh4.c`'s TCR write arm opened with `if (cpu->cd.sh.pclock == 0) { fatal("INTERNAL
ERROR: pclock must be set for this machine. Aborting."); exit(1); }`. One ordinary guest
store to `0xffd80010` ended the host process.

**It is a CLASS, not a machine list.** `cpu_sh.c:233-234` adds this device from
`if (cpu->cd.sh.cpu_type.arch == 4)`, so **the CPU brings the TMU and the BOARD brings the
clock**. Five registered SH machine types name an arch-4 CPU; only `machine_dreamcast.c:51`
(50 MHz) and `machine_landisk.c:81` (33.33 MHz) assign `pclock`. The other three inherit a
guard that kills the host, and so does every future arch-4 SH machine whose author does not
know a rule written down nowhere. That is why the fix is at the guard and not in three
machine files.

*Why four rounds of SH-4 `exit(1)` work walked past it:* the wording says
`INTERNAL ERROR ... Aborting`, which reads as a construction fault -- something that cannot
happen. It is reached by an ordinary store.

### THE BRIEF SAID TWO MACHINES. IT IS THREE, AND TWO SEATS CAUGHT IT INDEPENDENTLY

`machine_test.c:535` is `MACHINE_DEFAULT_CPU(baresh)`; `:541` is
`MACHINE_DEFAULT_CPU(testsh)`. The brief cited both line numbers and attributed them to one
machine, so **`baresh` -- a separately registered machine type -- was never named**.
Measured: `-E baresh` dies identically. A third seat additionally measured `-e jornada690`
reproducing (the subtype is never read, so it is the same code path) and confirmed all five
machines carry the device by reading `IPRD = 0xda74` on each.

The round's own prose said "2 of 4". The truth is **3 of 5**.

### The fix: decline the write, which is what the same function already does twenty lines down

`#447` had already answered the analogous question in this exact arm, and its comment is
explicit: *"substituting a prescaler for a clock source we cannot provide would be inventing
a rate. The guest can see the rejection by reading TCR back."* `#459` follows it -- once-only
diagnostic, `break`, no state touched -- using the eleventh `SH4_VAL_*` latch class.

**That eleventh class was free, and a seat found out why.** The carrier still carried
"convert the `SH4_VAL_*` defines to a C99 enum ending in `_NCLASS` ... apply that when a
tenth class arrives" as an OUTSTANDING obligation. It was already discharged --
`dev_sh4.c:124` is the enum, and the file's own comment records the pre-set trigger firing on
`SH4_VAL_SCICMD`. A stale instruction in the carrier is a future round redoing finished work,
so it is now marked complete.

### The guard stays above the prescaler switch — but for a SMALLER reason than first claimed

An earlier draft of this block said moving the decline lower would install *"a frequency the
guest never asked for"*, citing `#447`. **A pass-2 seat measured that this cannot happen at
this predicate.** `pclock == 0` makes all four prescaler cases yield `0.0`, and `timer_hz[]`
is *already* `0.0` — DEVINIT memsets the struct and those four cases are its only writes.
Nothing is installed and nothing changes. `#447`'s hazard is real where `pclock` is
**non-zero**; it does not transfer.

The real reason is **diagnostic consistency**: lower, the `debug()` line announces
`clock set to 0.000000 Hz` on a write that is then refused, and it is *unlatched*, so it
prints once per STORE where the decline prints once per TIMER. The seat built that mutant and
it scores **16/16** — four stores, four announcements of a rate never installed, no row sees
it. Filed as `sh4pclockquiet`.

*And `m_below` is a DIFFERENT mutant* — the missing `break`, which lets the write land and is
caught by `unlatch`. An earlier record attached it to the guard-position claim: two mutants
under one name, and **nothing in the kill table measures the guard's position**.

### THE HONEST COST HAS TWO HALVES, and the round demoted the first one too far

The design brief defended the trade as "a crash becomes a hang". A measuring seat corrected
that -- and then a pass-2 seat corrected the correction, which is the version that ships.

**(a) The stall remains the PRIMARY behavioural cost.** A guest that programs TCR and waits
for a TMU interrupt now waits forever where it used to die, and for automation that turns an
immediate nonzero exit into a possible timeout. **(b) ADDITIONALLY**, the diagnostic degrades
from unmissable to once-per-timer for the device lifetime. *(b) is an extra cost, not a
replacement for (a)* -- an intermediate draft said "the honest cost is the latch, NOT the
stall", which let the round off too easily.

The two grounds that DO narrow (a)'s practical reach today:

* **The hang is hypothetical in this tree.** `machine_hpcsh.c`'s `MACHINE_SETUP` body is
  commented out at `:48-64` -- and only the `hpc_bootinfo` half; what remains registers RAM
  mirrors and a dumb framebuffer, with no console wiring, no bootinfo and no disk, so **no
  guest boots on hpcsh at
  all**. *That narrows (a) ON HPCSH ONLY, and an earlier draft generalised past its own
  evidence:* `baresh` and `testsh` run hand-written test programs, and a program that
  programs TCR and polls TCNT **is** the hang — this round's own detector plants exactly
  such a program. The host death was measured everywhere; the stall is hypothetical on one
  machine of the three.
* **The real de-escalation cost is that the diagnostic degrades from unmissable to
  once-per-timer for the device lifetime.** A guest that spins programming TCR0 gets one
  line and then permanent silence, buried in a boot log. That is sharper and more accurate
  than "waits forever", and neither the brief nor the first draft said it.

What does survive: the counterfactual was never a working timer -- on these machines every
TCR write died, so nothing that worked is lost -- the guest can see the rejection by reading
TCR back (**measured `0x0` versus `0x20`**), and `fatal()` in this tree prints rather than
exits (`debugmsg.c:384-390`) and cannot be silenced by `-q`.

### THE ROUND SHIPPED A FALSE CLAIM ABOUT ITS OWN PANEL, AND THE MISCOUNTED SEAT CAUGHT IT

An earlier draft of the shipped comment read *"A panel of nine seats reached this 8-1."*
**It was written while the ninth seat was still running, and that seat then did not vote
B.** Counting a seat that has not answered is precisely the shape the seat ledger exists to
refuse, and it appeared inside a round whose whole subject is a guard nobody checked.

Corrected in place rather than silently superseded. The accurate statement: **all nine
answered, and all nine agree the decline is mandatory.** Seven say it is the whole fix. Two
would additionally assign a `pclock` to the SYNTHETIC machines, on the ground that a
fictional machine's parameters are the project's own *definition* rather than a hardware
*fact* -- a real argument that does not transfer to hpcsh. Held out as a CAPABILITY change
in a different file and semantic class, per the round-scope rule, and filed as
`sh4testclock`.

### The detector: 6/16 pre-fix, 16/16 post-fix

*The pre-fix number is measured against `git show HEAD:src/devices/dev_sh4.c` rebuilt into a
private tree, NOT against `build/`.* A seat reported that `build/gxemul`'s mtime moved
underneath it mid-review, so a run it believed was pre-fix was post-fix and the output could
not distinguish the two. **A seat asked to witness "on the committed build" while the loop is
implementing is measuring an undefined binary.** Rebuild from `git show HEAD:` or stamp it.

```
  the fix                                          16/16
  pre       HEAD, fatal + exit(1)                   6/16   all 6 kill/diag + all 4 observability
  m_silent  decline, no diagnostic                 12/15   says; once; pertmr
  m_flat    one latch instance for all timers      14/15   pertmr
  m_nolatch always print, no once-only             14/15   once
  m_below   declines but the write LANDS           14/15   unlatch
```

*The four mutants carry `/15` because they were measured before `accept dc tcr` was added;
they are not restated as `/16`, because they were not re-run at 16. The two `/16` rows are
the same script on both sides, which is what the witness clause requires.*

**THREE OF THE FOUR OBSERVABILITY ROWS ARE EACH THE SOLE KILLER OF ONE MUTANT** -- `pertmr`
alone catches a shared latch instance, `once` alone catches a missing latch, `unlatch` alone
catches a decline that lets the write land. That is the strongest justification a row can
carry, and none of the four existed until the round asked what a silent decline would cost.

**Two clock values, not one, and the second is the point.** A seat observed that a single
accept row pinned at landisk's 33.33 MHz is passed by a mutant that HARDCODES `33333333` in
place of `cpu->cd.sh.pclock` -- the row cannot tell "reads the machine's clock" from "happens
to agree with landisk". Dreamcast's 50 MHz is the discriminator.

**The de-escalation clause, discharged by measured kill.** The predicate that used to gate
death is exactly one, and a seat established it was **the last guest-reachable `exit(` in the device.** *The line numbers are deliberately omitted here, and that is the finding rather than laziness:* an earlier draft cited four, and the 15-line paragraph correcting the false panel claim -- added later in the same round -- shifted every one of them. **A comment that cites line numbers in its own file invalidates them each time it is edited.** What is stable is the structure: exactly four `exit(1);` remain in `dev_sh4.c`, one wrapped in `#ifdef SH4_DEBUG` and three on `interrupt_handler_lookup` construction failures. None is reachable by a guest. Its accept rows redden under a guard-only growth mutant -- `|| (pclock %
256) != 0`, in-idiom because it is `#447`'s own reasoning one level deeper. Guard-only is the
correct form here by the `#451` discriminator: **the latch operand is the constant `1`, which
the guard cannot feed**, so guard-only is non-equivalent AND quieter than the joint form.

### Two near-misses, in opposite directions, both caught by asking rule 4

* **False NEGATIVE.** The first probe run reported `testsh kill  survived` -- that testsh
  does not reproduce. It reused hpcsh's scratch address on a machine whose RAM is at physical
  0, so the instruction was never planted. A wrong address quietly NARROWS a live defect.
* **False POSITIVE.** The dreamcast accept row first read `died` -- **the same string the
  trigger rows produce**. Dreamcast brings up two console inputs (`SH4 SCIF` and `maple`) and
  `console.c:994-1007` makes that fatal without `-x`. Scored naively, a console-configuration
  failure would have become a fourth reproduction. `-x` routes through
  `console_allow_slaves()` (`console.c:943`); the early return it enables is `console.c:985`,
  and no xterm is spawned for a console never used.

*Both were caught by the same question -- did it fail for the reason under test -- and
neither by a size or liveness check.*

### Filed, not fixed

* `sh4testclock` -- give `baresh`/`testsh` a defined synthetic pclock. A seat measured
  `2^25 = 33554432` working, chosen because every TMU prescaler divides it exactly and
  nobody will mistake it for a Jornada measurement.
* `sh4cpudevscope` -- **the class this round is one symptom of.** The SH-4 on-chip block is
  added per-CPU but is machine-scoped. Two more symptoms measured: `-n 2 -E landisk` refuses
  to construct (`"sh4" collides with device 11`), and `dev_sh4.c` hardcodes
  `machine[0].cpu[0].irq[...]` for the TMU lookup.
* `sh4frqcr` -- `FRQCR` is modelled by `dev_sh4.c`'s `case SH4_CPG_FRQCR` as a bare latch
  with **no reset value** (`cpg_frqcr` is never initialised), so a guest reads `0x0000`, which is not a legal FRQCR value (Table 10.3 gives
  `H'0E1A`/`H'0E23`/`H'0E13`/`H'0E0A`). That is the register real hardware derives the
  peripheral clock FROM, and it is the honest long-run answer to "where should pclock come
  from".
* `hpcshcpu` -- **is hpcsh's CPU family even right?** `doc/TODO.html:322-323` groups hpcsh
  with `NetBSD/evbsh3` under "SH3-specific devices", while `machine_hpcsh.c:89` names SH7750
  (arch 4). *The repo contradicts itself and there is no SH-3 manual in `_scratchpad`.* Two
  seats independently refused to settle it from memory -- which is the `#357`/`#362`/`#365`
  citation failure not repeating. Obtain a source first.

### Option D was measured and rejected, which is worth more than declining it on reasoning

"Give hpcsh an arch-3 CPU so the device is never added" removes the defect at its root, and a
seat measured that it works: `-C SH7708R -e jornada680` needs no rebuild, the store hits
`non-existant paddr`, the host survives, and the startup banner is byte-identical except the
CPU name.

**Rejected anyway, on what arch-3 actually removes.** `dev_sh4.c` is not "the timer" -- it is
CCN/MMU, INTC, TMU, RTC, BSC, DMAC, SCIF, the TLB arrays and the PCIC. An arch-3 hpcsh has
none of it. `cpu_sh.c:527-533` shows both SH-3 interrupt handlers are `/* TODO */` stubs that
silently drop asserts, and `cpu_sh.c:224` uses a **leftover UTLB loop counter** as
`templ.line`, inert today only because that handler is a stub. `cpu_sh.c:33` says it plainly:
*"TODO: This actually only works or SH4 so far, not SH3."* Changing a machine's modelled CPU
family on contested evidence, to route around a device bug, is a much larger claim than the
bug warrants.

## Round 458 (#458) -- the interrupt priority table consulted two registers out of four

`sh_update_interrupt_priorities()` read `intc_ipra` and `intc_intpri08` and nothing
else. Table 19.6 (`_scratchpad/sh7750_hardware.txt:40231`) assigns four sources to each
of IPRA-IPRD. So IPRB and IPRC were stored by the device, passed to this function, and
ignored -- **and even IPRA was read incompletely**: TMU0/1/2 were handled and RTC in
bits [3:0] was not, leaving a source in a register this function DOES consult
permanently at priority 0.

### SCIF was sourced from a register that does not exist, and five things say so

The model took SCIF's priority from `intc_intpri08 >> 16`. It belongs in **IPRC[7:4]**:

* Table 19.5 (`:40036`) gives it per-source at `:40142`: `SCIF ERI H'700 ... IPRC (7-4)`.
* Table 19.6 (`:40231`) agrees.
* The SH-4 programming manual 5.6 lists SCIF among the modules whose levels are set
  "in the interrupt priority registers (IPRA-IPRC)".
* **This tree's own header says so** -- `sh4_intcreg.h:91`, `IPRC_SCIF_MASK 0x00f0`.
  The code contradicted a header sitting beside it.
* A full enumeration of the manual returns `INTPRI00` **sixteen times and no other
  INTPRI register at all**. INTPRI00 is SH7750R-only and covers TMU3/TMU4. The layout
  the code used is the SH7760's, which `cpu_sh_init`'s own comment admits, and no
  SH7760 appears in `SH_CPU_TYPE_DEFS`.

**And the register was never even mapped.** `SH4_INTPRI00` is `0xfe080000`, outside the
single registered window (`SH4_REG_BASE` + 0x01000000), so `dev_sh4.c`'s INTPRI cases
are unreachable and `intc_intpri08` kept its init value forever. A guest store to it
reports `non-existant paddr`. SCIF's priority was a guest-immutable constant 3.

### The citations were re-read before shipping, and two were wrong

`#457` shipped four wrong citations. This round checked every one against the file
before commit, and **two of its own were wrong**:

* The per-source table is **19.5** ("Interrupt Exception Handling Sources and Priority
  Order", `:40036`), not 19.4. Table 19.4 is `:39965`, "SH7750 IRL3-IRL0 Pins and
  Interrupt Levels (When IRLM = 1)" -- which turns out to be the *correct* citation for
  the IPRD argument below, so the right reference was in hand and attached to the wrong
  claim.
* Table 19.6's heading is `:40231`; the comment said `:40230`, the line above it.

**And one apparent error was not one.** `pdftotext -layout` staggers a vertically-centered
table cell onto the wrong line, so Table 19.5 extracts as `ATI H'480 / H'4A0 / PRI H'4C0 /
CUI` -- which reads as *PRI = H'4C0* and would have condemned three correct constants. The
SCI block four rows below is the decoder: `sh4_exception.h:93-96` already pins SCI
ERI/RXI/TXI/TEI at `0x4e0/0x500/0x520/0x540` in shipped code, and that reconciles with the
extraction **only** if names and codes pair strictly in order down each column. Applying
that rule to RTC gives `0x480/0x4a0/0x4c0`, which is what the code says. DMTE0 and DMAE are
confirmed a second time by an unstaggered table at `:32655`.

*This matters more than a wrong page number: a wrong INTEVT constant is invisible to the
probe, because the probe reads the same constant. The check has to come from outside the
code.* The rule is now in the carrier.

### A rung-4 boot witness: the guest asks for 12 and gets 3

Instrumenting a 90-second `-E landisk` boot of `openbsd76-landisk-bsd.rd`: the guest
writes **`IPRC = 0x00c0`** -- SCIF priority **12** -- at the moment `scif0: cons`
attaches, and the model delivered priority **3** on all fifteen SCIF asserts of that
boot. Full IPR trace: `IPRA 0x0300 -> 0xe300`, `IPRC 0x00c0`, `IPRD 0x0000`, IPRB and
INTPRI never written.

That also answers the de-escalation question this round had to ask before touching
anything: re-sourcing SCIF to IPRC is safe *because* the guest programs IPRC. Both
builds boot to the installer prompt at ~2.886e9 instructions. Dreamcast is an honest
UNKNOWN -- no image in `_images/`, and SCIF is not its console.

### *** IPRD IS DELIBERATELY NOT READ, and that is measured rather than cautious ***

"Read all four registers per Table 19.6" is the obvious design and it is **wrong**.
IPRD sets per-pin IRL priorities in IRLM=1 mode, which `dev_sh4.c` refuses outright, so
it can never be in effect. And its four nibbles ALIAS live slots: IRL0-3 are
`0x240/0x2a0/0x300/0x360`, which are also IRQ2/5/8/11 -- owned by the hardwired loop and
used today by the PCIC lines and the dreamcast ASIC.

Measured: one guest `IPRD := 0` -- **the exact store OpenBSD/landisk 7.6 makes during
boot** -- drops those four slots from `0xd/0xa/0x7/0x4` to zero, masking four PCIC lines
permanently, while a control slot not in IPRD (IRQ10, the wdc) is untouched. A variant
reading IPRD scores the same as this one, so reading it buys nothing and costs that.

*** AND THE MANUAL CORROBORATES IT FROM AN ANGLE THE DESIGN DID NOT USE. *** IPRA-IPRC
reset to `H'0000`, but **IPRD resets to `H'DA74`** -- stated three times independently
(`:39856`, `:40194`, `:48567`). Those nibbles are `13/10/7/4`. The hardwired loop at
`cpu_sh.c:352` computes `15 - ((i - SH4_INTEVT_IRQ0) / 0x20)`, which hands IRQ2/5/8/11 --
the slots IRL0-3 alias -- exactly **13/10/7/4**. *The model is already sitting on the
hardware's IPRD reset state for all four lines, matching nibble for nibble.*

So reading IPRD could not improve the reset case even in principle; it could only let a
guest write move the model AWAY from a correct default, which is precisely what the
measured `IPRD := 0` does. Whether upstream chose that descending ramp to make the IRL
defaults come out right, or whether it fell out, is not determinable from the code -- the
agreement is recorded as measured, not as intent.

### The naive witness is GREEN on the unfixed build

The obvious row -- write one IPR, expect delivery -- **passes HEAD**. It fails vacuity
floor clause (a) outright and has zero discriminating power. It ships as a LABELLED row
so nobody re-invents it. What discriminates is IMASK BRACKETING: delivery needs
`IMASK < int_level`, so a pair of rows at different IMASK pins the level to a range
rather than to "nonzero".

### Two mutants no behavioural row could ever catch

```
  the fix                                       18/18
  m_iprconly    RTC + IPRB mapping dropped      10/12   iprb wdt; ipra rtc
  m_nortc       three RTC lines dropped         11/12   ipra rtc
  m_norescan    rescan call dropped             11/12   raise
  m_iprdread    reads all four IPRs             13/14   iprd hold
  m_sciftxonly  SCIF loop narrowed to TXI       15/18   scif eri; scif rxi; scif bri
```

*The denominators are the detector's size WHEN EACH WAS MEASURED, and they are not restated
upward, because the mutants were not re-run at 18. The detector grew twice during pass 2 —
the `iprd hold`/`iprd ctl` pair at 12->14, then the SCIF membership rows at 14->18 — and each
growth was forced by a mutant the previous size could not see. `m_sciftxonly`'s own line
records both facts: it scored a clean 14/14 before those four rows existed.*

*`scif txi` stays GREEN under `m_sciftxonly`, which is the point — the mutant does still map
TXI. Three of four red is what "the loop lost its other members" looks like.*

Every mutant is reddened by exactly the row built for it and nothing else.

`m_iprconly` (drop the RTC and IPRB blocks) and `m_nortc` (drop the three RTC lines)
each scored a **clean 10/10** against every behavioural row -- not because the rows are
weak, but because **WDT, REF, SCI, GPIO, DMAC, H-UDI and RTC have no `INTERRUPT_ASSERT`
anywhere in this tree.** Nothing a guest can DO depends on their priorities.

So `#458` exposes `int_prio_and_pending[]`, `int_to_assert` and `int_level` through the
settings interface, and two rows read the table directly: after a guest `IPRB := 0xa000`
the WDT slot must read `0xa`, and after `IPRA := 0x000c` the RTC slot must read `0xc`.
**Those two rows are the reason the exposure exists**; without them it is an unused
convenience.

*The widths are matched to the declarations rather than guessed -- `int_to_assert` is
`int16_t` and `int_level` is `unsigned int`. These macros take the variable's ADDRESS,
so a mismatched width reads neighbouring bytes and reports a plausible wrong number.*

### What this round does NOT claim

`scifonly` and `ipronly` measured **byte for byte identical**, which means the entire
behaviourally-witnessable payload of the register half is the SCIF re-source. IPRA[3:0],
IPRB and the rest make the model's table agree with the manual for sources nothing can
currently raise. That is worth doing -- a priority table that silently disagrees with the
hardware is a trap for whoever next wires up a device -- but it is a judgement about
scope, not a measurement, and this record says so rather than claiming those nibbles
witnessed.

### *** THE SCOPE RULING WAS OVERTAKEN BY AN IMPLEMENTATION FACT, and an earlier draft of
this block recorded BOTH halves of the contradiction without noticing. ***

The brief proposed merging `sh4iprbcd` with `sh4prioraise`; a pass-1 seat refused, on three
grounds including that **the project had already adjudicated it** -- the `sh4prioraise`
filing itself says "a second design question, its own round". That refusal was accepted, and
this block said "sh4prioraise is NOT in this round" *in the same breath as* "the rescan half
IS present" and "the row that isolates it, `raise`, is red on an IPR-only build". Both
sentences were true. Together they say the round ships the fix, ships a row for it, and
denies doing so.

**A pass-2 seat named the implementation fact that settles it:** rewriting priority nibbles
of a table that may already hold a pending request leaves `int_to_assert` stale, so the
rescan is load-bearing *for the register fix itself*, not an optional companion. The two
were separable as filings and are not separable as code. So `sh4prioraise` closes on this
commit: the rescan call ships, `raise`/`raise_lo` pin it, and `m_norescan` reddens `raise`
alone.

*Recorded as a scope CHANGE rather than quietly merged, because the earlier ruling was
correct on the evidence it had.* What it could not know was that `rescanonly` would measure
identical to `pre` -- the rescan fixes nothing observable ALONE -- which is precisely why it
cannot be deferred to a later round without leaving this one's table able to go stale.

The standing-LOWER direction is NOT closed: no row asserts at a high priority and then
lowers it while the request stands. Filed as `sh4standinglower` with the one-line kill row
a seat supplied.

### The ask-again earned its keep, on the round's own central decision

Project rule: once a kill table is clean, ask the panel once more -- **capped at one ask
per detector per round**. The first table was clean at 12/12, and the ask returned a
finding that the round could not have reached alone:

> *"None of the 12 rows writes IPRD except `devsig`, a read of the reset value. A
> well-meaning 'read all four registers' mutant is predicted 12/12 and would still smash
> landisk PCIC. That is the hole, not the design."*

**The IPRD decision -- the most-argued call in this round -- was defended only by a
comment.** `iprd hold` and `iprd ctl` now defend it: a guest `IPRD := 0` must leave
IRQ2/IRL0 (`0x240`) at `0xd`, while IRQ10 (`0x340`), outside IPRD, stays `0x5` under fix
and mutant alike. That control is what makes a red attributable to IPRD rather than to a
broken session. **Measured, not predicted: `m_iprdread` scores 13/14, red on `iprd hold`
alone.**

Five seats separately named the other escape family -- delete any single mapping line for
a slot no row reads, and the detector scores full marks (H-UDI, GPIO, RTC PRI/CUI, the REF
pair, the DMAC loop, the SCI loop, `<=`->`<` on SCI TEI, and a wrong-DESTINATION variant
that transposes the GPIO and H-UDI nibbles). All **FILED** as `sh4iprunpinned`, following
`#447`: hypothetical edits in uncovered product cells, against a detector measured above
the vacuity floor, are coverage debt. The cap is the anti-`#392` clause and it held.

### *** THE ASK-AGAIN'S REAL PRIZE: ONE ESCAPE THAT WAS NOT COVERAGE DEBT. ***

Every escape above reaches a slot nothing in this tree asserts. The measuring seat found
one that does not, and **measured it at 14/14** — one identifier in the round's own IPRC
block:

```c
for (i=SH4_INTEVT_SCIF_ERI; i<=SH4_INTEVT_SCIF_TXI; i+=0x20)   /* ship   */
for (i=SH4_INTEVT_SCIF_TXI; i<=SH4_INTEVT_SCIF_TXI; i+=0x20)   /* mutant */
```

**SCIF RXI (`0x720`) is LIVE.** `dev_sh4.c:250-256` asserts `scif_rx_irq` whenever
`SCSCR2.RIE && SCSSR2.DR`, connected at `:1912`. That is **console input on landisk** — the
only SH machine this project boots. Measured at `IPRC=0x00f0`, `SCSCR2=0x40`, `SCSSR2=0x01`,
`IMASK=3`:

| | `iprio_720` | RX delivery |
|---|---|---|
| the fix | `0x1f` — asserted, priority 15 | **delivered** |
| `m_sciftxonly` | `0x10` — asserted, priority **0** | **refused** |

So the mutant silently deletes console input and the detector stays green. The ten
behavioural rows all drive **TXI**: `scif_assert_code()` writes `SCSCR2.TIE` +
`SCSSR2.TDFE|TEND`, which is the TX arm. Nothing ever touched the RX side.

**This is a MEASURED FALSE PASS on live functionality, so the stopping rule licenses fixing
it in-round** — and it is the de-escalation clause's own shape: the round was pinning the
accept side of a four-member loop at exactly one member. Four rows now pin the loop's whole
membership in one session, which kills *every* narrowing of it rather than the one measured.

**A second measured result from the same seat is worth keeping:** `m_irqramp` (`15 -` ->
`14 -` in the hardwired ramp, which masks IRQ14 and lowers every IRQ line by one) **passes
the twelve-row detector** and scores 12/14 against the current one — killed by the two IPRD
rows. Those rows earn their keep well beyond the IPRD question they were added for.

### The gate caught a malformed edit to the gate, which is the safe direction

The first run of the finished gate came back **FAIL, 1 of 111**, with all eighteen `#458`
rows green and one failing check named **`n`**. A backslash-continuation written through a
nested heredoc had produced the two characters `
` in the `for v in ...` word list, adding
a bogus word, so the gate dutifully checked for a row called `n` and did not find one.

*Worth recording because it is the opposite of the padded-column trap this project already
knows.* A name that is too long makes its check **unsatisfiable and silent**; a name list
that gains junk fails **loudly and immediately**. Both are real, and this one is safe by
construction. The word list is now one line with no continuations, and the two-second check
— expand it in `bash -c` and count — is in the carrier.

### Three things this round changes that are not the defect

* **SCIF's reset priority moves from 3 to 0, and that is correct.** `intc_intpri08` was
  initialised to `0x33333333`, so SCIF sat at priority 3 out of reset; IPRA-IPRC reset to
  `H'0000`, which is what hardware does. Any SH4 guest that enables SCIF interrupts
  *without* programming IPRC now gets nothing where it previously got delivery at 3. landisk
  programs IPRC — the boot witness shows it — and `machine_test.c` is the only other SH
  machine in the tree, so nothing under test regresses. Recorded now rather than discovered.
* **The rescan lift is not behaviourally verbatim.** `sh_cpu_interrupt_assert()` selects with
  `int_to_assert == 0 || prio > int_level`; the rescan selects with `prio > int_level` from a
  zeroed base, ascending index. Running it on every IPR write therefore RE-ARBITRATES, and
  ties resolve to the lowest INTEVT code. *Within* an IPR group that matches Table 19.5's
  "Default Priority within IPR Setting Unit" column exactly; *across* groups it does not
  (19.5 ranks SCIF `0x700` above WDT `0x560`; the scan picks WDT). Unwitnessable today, and
  pre-existing in the deassert path — but this diff makes that path run far more often.
* **The nine new `SH_INTEVT_*` are defined in `cpu_sh.c`, not in the header where they
  belong.** Deliberate: `src/include/thirdparty/sh4_exception.h` is byte-identical to
  pristine upstream and the fork has never edited it. Keeping a thirdparty header pristine
  outweighs table locality.

### One seat's headline was wrong, and checking it took two minutes

A packet-fed seat required, as its condition to ship, that the SCIF loop be changed from
`i<=SH4_INTEVT_SCIF_TXI` to `i<=SH4_INTEVT_SCIF_TEI`, calling the current form an
off-by-one that leaves SCIF TEI at priority 0. **`SH4_INTEVT_SCIF_TEI` does not exist.**
`sh4_exception.h:104-107` defines exactly four SCIF vectors -- ERI `0x700`, RXI `0x720`,
**BRI** `0x740`, TXI `0x760` -- so the loop already covers all four and the suggested edit
would not compile. The seat had transplanted SCI's vector set (which does end in TEI, at
`0x540`) onto SCIF. Recorded because the seat was right about everything else, and a
confident wrong headline from an otherwise-good seat is the failure mode the panel exists
to absorb.

### One new sibling, confirmed by arithmetic

`dev_sh4.c` wires 16 PCIC lines as `SH4_INTEVT_IRQ0 + 0x20 * i`, so **line 15 lands on
`0x3e0`** -- the line #456 established the priority loop never assigns and which appears
nowhere in the manual. PCIC interrupt 15 can never be delivered. Same class as #456,
different device.

## Round 457 (#457) -- three guest stores ended the host process

`dev_sh4.c` raises `sh_exception(cpu, EXPEVT_RESET_TLB_MULTI_HIT, 0, 0)` when a guest
ASSOCIATIVE write to the UTLB address array matches more than one entry.
`sh_exception()` had no case for `0x140`, so it fell to `default:` and ran `exit(1)`.

The fix is one `case` label joining the existing reset group. **Table 5.2 Exceptions**
(`_scratchpad/sh7750_hardware.txt:11994`, rows at `:12006`/`:12010`) puts both TLB
multiple-hit exceptions in Reset/Abort, vector `H'A000 0000`, code `H'140` -- the same
rows as power-on and manual reset. `EXPEVT` survives grouping because the common code
assigns it BEFORE the switch.

**Deleting the detection was the brief's own favoured reading and is REFUTED** by
3.7.4 (`:10141-10143`), which both raises the exception and supplies the ordering:
*"D and V specified in the data field are written to that entry. If there is more than
one matching entry, a data TLB multiple hit exception results."* Write first, then
raise -- so update-before-count is faithful and a proposed scan-first rewrite would be
less so.

### 1/6 pre-fix, 6/6 post-fix, and the single-hit control is GREEN PRE-FIX

That last part is what makes the deaths meaningful: the control runs the same three
stores with a different VPN on entry 1, so it proves the program executes and the
session survives it. The kill is the SECOND match, not the code.

### Six mutants, and three are each killed by exactly ONE row

```
the fix                              6/6
mutA  detection deleted              2/6   four rows
mutB  own arm -> general vector      3/6   three rows
mutC  own arm, pc + vbr only         5/6   tlbm sr     ALONE
mutD  n_hits > 2                     2/6   four rows
mutE  device raises RESET_MANUAL     5/6   tlbm expevt ALONE
mutF  n_hits >= 1                    5/6   tlbm single ALONE
```

**A survival-only oracle passes all six.** `expevt` + `pc` kills four and is passed by
mutC and mutF.

`mutC` is the one worth remembering, and it is a likelier implementation than the fix
itself -- a maintainer reading "a reset is executed" and writing their own arm that
sets `pc` and `vbr`. It is invisible to `alive`, `expevt`, `pc` AND `vbr`, because the
group's third statement is a **no-op from the reset-default SR** (IMASK already `0xf`,
FD already clear). Only pre-setting SR to `0x40008000` makes it observable. Figure 5.2
(`:12228`) specifies `SR.{MD,RB,BL,FD,IMASK} <- 11101111` for the transition, so that
statement is required rather than decoration.

**landisk, not testsh, and that is forced:** landisk's PROM leaves `vbr = 0x8c000000`
(`promemul/sh_ipl_g.c:55`), so `vbr == 0` is a real transition. Cold-start `vbr` on
testsh is already 0, which would make that row vacuous there.

### The comment shipped wrong four times over, and a seat opened every citation

FOURTH CONSECUTIVE ROUND where the code was right first time and the records were not.
All four verified by opening the file:

* **Table 5.1 -> Table 5.2.** `:12006` is in Table 5.2 Exceptions; Table 5.1 is
  *Exception-Related Registers*. The rows were right, the table number sent a reader
  to the wrong page.
* **3.7.2 -> 3.7.4.** `:10143` is *UTLB Address Array*; 3.7.2 is *ITLB Data Array 1* --
  which this session had already read, and mis-cited anyway.
* **"Manual_reset() line for line" is false.** That routine is ten statements including
  `Initialize_CPU()`; this arm is three. And NOT reinitialising is the faithful part:
  3.6.4's software processing inspects the UTLB entries after the reset.
* **The PPN sentence was the wrong warrant.** 3.6.4 says PPN *may* be corrupted; the
  device loop writes V and D and never touches PPN. The conclusion held; the reason did
  not, and a wrong reason gets reused.

Two residuals FILED, not fixed: TEA is never set (3.6.4 step 1 says it should be, and
*which* address is right for this route is a genuine UNKNOWN), and `cpu_sh.c` uses
`EXPEVT_RESET_POWER` where the manual specifies manual-reset for the BL-set case.

Gate 10 PASS at 89 checks -- 62 at the start of this session. Build rc=0, zero
warnings, four trees cmp-identical.

## Round 456 (#456) -- the SH test machine could not deliver an interrupt at all

`machine_test.c` wired the ENTIRE SH test-machine interrupt tree to
`SH4_INTEVT_IRQ15` (`0x3e0`). That line can never carry a priority: the loop in
`sh_update_interrupt_priorities()` stops at `IRQ14`, and its own formula
`15 - ((i - IRQ0) / 0x20)` yields **0** for `0x3e0` regardless -- so widening the loop
would not help, it would only assign zero to the encoding the manual calls "no
request". Priority 0 means masked. Nothing that machine raised could ever arrive.

The hardware has no such source either. SH7750 Hardware Manual Rev.7.00 19.2.2
(`_scratchpad/sh7750_hardware.txt:39908-39910`): *"A value of 15 (1111) indicates no
interrupt request (interrupt priority level 0)"*, and Table 19.5's IRL block ends at
`H'3C0`. **`H'3E0` appears nowhere in 50,853 lines.**

The fix is one identifier: `SH4_INTEVT_IRQ14`, the lowest REAL level, which is the
right tier for a catch-all -- least preemptive, and an IRL encoding is the honest
namespace for an external `irqc`.

### It ships immediately behind #455 because #455 made it SILENT

Until yesterday this was loud: priority 0 ran `exit(1)`, so any interrupt on the test
machine ended the host. `#455` correctly made priority 0 mean masked, per the manual --
and the same defect went from **loudly unusable to silently unusable**. That is the
de-escalation hazard in its literal form, which is why the row was filed in the same
breath as `#455` rather than found later.

### *** THE FIX INVALIDATED TWO OF #455's OWN ROWS, AND IT DID SO SILENTLY ***

`#455`'s `prio0 kill` / `prio0 quiet` worked **because** the test machine's line was
priority 0. Move it to priority 1 and a store there no longer reaches the priority-0
arm at all -- while the rows go on passing.

MEASURED, not predicted. A build carrying IRQ14 **and a verbatim reinstatement of
#455's kill** scores **5/7 with both rows GREEN**; the same kill on an IRQ15 build
scores **3/7 with both RED**. One identifier apart. And the fix itself is 7/7, so
nothing would have forced anyone to notice.

**Retargeting them to another priority-0 source is not available, and that was measured
rather than assumed.** SCIF asserts synchronously inside a guest store but sits at
priority 3 (`intc_intpri08` initialises to `0x33333333`) and the register that would
lower it is unmapped -- `non-existant paddr=0xfe080008`. The TMU on `testsh` dies on
*every* build with `pclock must be set for this machine`. **After #456 the test machine
has no guest-reachable priority-0 interrupt source at all.**

So the session machinery is kept and the rows' PURPOSE changes: they now pin that a
legal priority-1 interrupt IS delivered, which is #456's own claim. `#455`'s
priority-0 coverage moves to the landisk TMU rows, which still redden on that same
reinstatement -- confirmed, so the vacuity floor still holds.

### The kill table, and each row kills a family the other cannot

```
the fix (IRQ14)                     7/7
M1  revert to IRQ15                 6/7   irq14 deliv ALONE
M2  IRQ13 -- delivers, wrong level   6/7   irq14 imask ALONE
M3  IRQ0  -- delivers, wrong level   6/7   irq14 imask ALONE
pre-fix probe (IRQ15)               6/7   irq14 deliv
```

A delivery-only witness is passed by **any of IRQ0..IRQ13** -- a measuring seat built
IRQ13 and watched it escape before `irq14 imask` existed. Delivery needs
`IMASK < int_level`, so a level-1 line is admitted at IMASK 0 and refused at IMASK 1;
running both brackets the level to exactly 1. That is what pins IRQ14 specifically
rather than "some line delivered".

### Records corrected in the same commit

`sh_intprio_probe.py`'s header explained at length that the testsh route reaches the
priority-0 kill *because* the tree is wired to IRQ15, and quoted the abort line. That
became false the moment this shipped. The old text is KEPT rather than deleted, with
the correction beside it, because a future reader who finds that explanation in a git
log needs to see where it stopped being true.

The probe's rows also hardcoded `#455` in their output column; the two new rows would
have claimed a round they were never part of. Rows now name their own round.

Gate 10 PASS at 80 checks. Build rc=0, zero warnings, all four trees cmp-identical.

## Round 455 (#455) -- an interrupt at priority 0 ended the host process

`sh_cpu_interrupt_assert()` ran `fatal()` then `exit(1)` when the asserted line's
priority nibble was zero, under the comment *"Interrupt not implemented? Hm."*

**Nothing is unimplemented.** Priority 0 is documented, guest-selectable and the
RESET DEFAULT. SH7750 Hardware Manual Rev.7.00 19.2, p. 828
(`_scratchpad/sh7750_hardware.txt:39887`): *"When level 0 is set, the interrupt is
masked and interrupt requests are ignored."* And 19.3.1 (`:40193`): *"IPRA to IPRC
are initialized to H'0000 ... by a reset."* `cpu_sh_init` already reproduces that,
commenting *"All others are zero"*. So every on-chip source is masked out of reset
and one ordinary guest store ended the host.

The fix is a bare `return`.

### The witness is one store, and finding the right one took three corrections to this project's own rule

Measured on the committed build, `-E testsh`, unmodified, under `step 1`:

```
80010000:  2102        mov.l   r0,@r1  ; r1 = 0xb10000a0
[ SH interrupt 0x3e0, prio 0 (?), aborting ]
```

`machine_test.c` wires the entire test-machine interrupt tree to `SH4_INTEVT_IRQ15`
(`0x3e0`, index 31). `sh_update_interrupt_priorities()`'s loop is bounded
`i <= SH4_INTEVT_IRQ14`, so index 31 is never assigned -- and extending it would not
help, because the loop's own formula `15 - ((i - IRQ0) / 0x20)` yields 0 for that
line. `dev_irqc.c` defaults to all interrupts enabled. **So the SH test machine's
interrupt controller could not be used at all, and no guest register write could
prevent it.**

*** THE OBVIOUS ROUTE WOULD HAVE PRODUCED A VACUOUS WITNESS, AND THE RULE THAT SAID
OTHERWISE WAS THIS PROJECT'S OWN, WRITTEN THE SAME DAY. *** A TMU underflow also
reaches the kill, and the carrier had just been updated to say that the assert path
is visible under stepping -- true, and verified. But a TMU underflow is produced by a
HOST timer, and `debugger.c:800` calls `timer_stop()` *"while interacting with the
user"* with the step command returning at `:835-836` **before** `timer_start()` at
`:840`. Host timers are stopped for the whole `step N`; the tick loop runs but finds
nothing pending. **A step-based timer row would have scored a correct pre-fix build
ALIVE and failed vacuity floor clause (a) in silence.** A review seat caught it in
the design.

> The rule now carries its discriminator: a step probe sees a **synchronous** assert
> -- a device handler reached inside the guest's own load or store -- and not one fed
> by a host-timer callback. Ask what produces the thing the tick consumes.

Three passes over one sentence, each narrower than the last.

### Two controls, and one of them exposed a defect in the probe's own parser

Clause (ii) needs a LIVENESS control and a DEVICE-SIGNATURE control, because one is
not enough -- the footbridge probe's first draft returned `0x0` everywhere with its
RAM control green. Here the signature is a guest load of `DEV_MP_MEMORY`, which
answers `ram_mb * 1048576` on the same device the witness pokes: a value RAM at that
address cannot produce.

**It caught a byte-order defect in the probe, and the liveness row had been hiding
it.** `dump` prints bytes in memory order and this CPU is little-endian, so the
digits must be swapped; the first draft compared the raw string. Its liveness row
passed anyway, because the value chosen was `0x5a5a5a5a` -- **a palindrome under byte
swap**. The device-signature row is what exposed it: `0x04000000` came back as
`0x00000004`. The liveness value is now asymmetric.

*A control value must be ASYMMETRIC or it cannot see this class at all. That is the
hand-assembled encoding trap in a different disguise -- the same reason every
instruction probe needs a row expecting a small nonzero value in a specific register.*

The first draft also reused landisk's scratch address on `testsh`, whose RAM is at
physical 0, so the liveness row read back `0x00000000`. **This project has now made
that exact mistake twice on testsh**, the earlier one in a pclock witness.

Pre-fix 2/4, post-fix 4/4, both controls green in both directions.

### The kill table

```
the fix                             7/7
M1  verbatim reinstatement          2/4   kill + quiet
M2  drop exit(), keep the print     3/4   quiet ALONE
M3' partial fix, only index 31      4/6   tmu + tmuq ONLY  (4/4 before they existed)
M4  clears SH_INT_ASSERTED          4/4   ESCAPES -- filed
M5  guard deleted entirely          4/4   ESCAPES -- filed
G1  growth: prio <= 1               6/7   accept ALONE
pristine 0.7.0, null medium         2/4
```

### What is deliberately NOT printed

The `sh4_val_first` latch idiom that #438, #441, #443, #447 and #449 all use does not
apply here, and the distinction is the point: that family answers *"the guest asked
for a feature this model does not implement"*, while a masked interrupt is **correct
guest behaviour** that a kernel performs routinely during early boot. A latched
diagnostic would fire on it. And `fatal()` has no `quiet_mode` early-out
(`debugmsg.c:384-390`), so it could not be silenced with `-q` either.

### `SH_INT_ASSERTED` is left set, and that is required rather than merely defensible

The manual settles it: 19.4.1 says the controller selects the highest-priority request
and *"lower-priority interrupts are held pending"*, and the request is a level driven
by the peripheral's source flag until software clears it. **"Ignored" is not
"discarded."** Masking blocks acceptance, not the request.

Clearing the bit would additionally make `sh4prioraise` -- filed, and a genuine defect
-- **unfixable**, because a later rescan would find nothing to deliver. Two seats
reached that independently.

### Filed with the fix, because this fix makes one of them silent

* **`sh4irq15`** -- `machine_test.c` selects the one INTEVT line that is priority 0 by
  construction. After #455, `-E testsh` goes from LOUDLY unusable to SILENTLY unusable,
  which is the de-escalation hazard in literal form. One identifier; its own round.
* **`sh4tlbmulti`** -- NEW, found by a records seat sweeping for siblings rather than
  by looking for it: `sh_exception()` has no case for `EXPEVT_RESET_TLB_MULTI_HIT`, so a
  guest UTLB write producing two matching entries falls to `default:` and ends the host.
  Same family, same file.
* **`sh4iprbcd`**, latent only because nothing asserts those lines today -- which is the
  condition #455 shows can change.
* **`sh4prioraise`**. *Corrected 2026-08-22: an earlier draft of this line called it
  latent too. It is NOT.* TMU0-2 and SCIF DO assert in-tree, so a guest that asserts
  while masked and then raises IPRA hits it today -- a periodic TMU degrades to a
  one-period delay, but a one-shot like SCIF RXI withholds delivery until the next
  byte arrives. The ledger's own per-row note had the careful form ("#455 makes it
  reachable rather than fatal"); this sentence was the loose one.

## Round 454 (#454) -- the store-queue flush is judged READ type, and a shipped gate row pinned the opposite

`X(pref_rn)` passed `FLAG_WRITEFLAG` when flushing a store queue through the UTLB.
The manual says read type. Two copies of it now sit in the tree and both say so in
the same words -- SH7750 Hardware Manual Rev.7.00 4.7.4 "SQ Protection", p. 144
(`_scratchpad/sh7750_hardware.txt:11744-11746`), and the SH-4 programming manual
4.6.4 (`sh4_programming.txt:3561-3563`):

> "Write type exception judgment is performed for writes to the SQs, and **read
> type for transfer from the SQs to external memory (PREF instruction)**, and a TLB
> miss exception, protection violation exception, or initial page write exception is
> generated."

The fix is one token: `FLAG_WRITEFLAG` becomes `0`. This tree has no `FLAG_READFLAG`;
a read is the absence of the bit, exactly as `memory_rw.c:249` builds it.

### The detector pinned the defect, so correcting the code would have turned it red

`gate_sh_rounding.sh` said so in as many words: *"a build that judged this access as
a read would complete the copy and fail this row alone."* It would have. That is a
detector enforcing a defect, which is worse than no detector.

*** RE-PINNING AN ORACLE IS OBSERVATIONALLY IDENTICAL TO FITTING THE TEST TO THE
BINARY, so the order is the warrant. *** The rows were re-pinned FIRST and measured
RED on the COMMITTED build, before any source edit existed:

```
COMMITTED build, re-pinned oracle:                    26/31
  sq pr00 rdok   got 0xdeadbeef   want 0xa0000000,0xa0000001   FAIL
  sq d0 rdok     got 0xdeadbeef   want 0xa0000000,0xa0000001   FAIL
  sq miss evt    got 0x00000060   want 0x00000040              FAIL
  sq pr00 evt    got 0x000000c0   want 0x00000999              FAIL
  sq d0 evt      got 0x00000080   want 0x00000999              FAIL
FIXED build, same rows:                               31/31
```

The pass-1 panel proposed that order after the brief proposed the reverse, and it is
adopted generally as the ORACLE-CORRECTION RULE. The old pin had no provenance to
overturn: its own comment says it pinned "the WRITE-type judgement the panel split
on" -- a verdict, not a document.

### It settled a filed question as a side effect

`sh4sqexpevt` recorded, as reading rather than measurement, that all three of 4.7.4's
exceptions are raised. The pre-fix EXPEVT column above is that measurement: 0x060
(store-type miss), 0x0c0 (protection violation, store) and 0x080 (initial page write).

### Two one-token escapes were MEASURED against the value rows, and both scored full marks

The copy channel cannot see this change once the transfer completes either way, so
the rows were extended to the exception channel and to the ITLB.

| mutant at the call site | rows | killed by |
|---|---|---|
| the fix (`0`) | 31/31 | -- |
| `FLAG_WRITEFLAG`, verbatim reinstatement | 26/31 | all five |
| `FLAG_NOEXCEPTIONS` | 30/31 | `sq miss evt` alone |
| `FLAG_INSTR` | 29/31 | the two `itlb` rows alone |
| pristine 0.7.0, null medium | 4/31 | nine rows |

`FLAG_NOEXCEPTIONS` is the one worth remembering: `translate_via_mmu`'s `exception:`
label returns **2 with `*return_paddr = 0`**, which the caller reads as success, so a
TLB miss lands the 32-byte payload at **physical address 0** in silence. Vacuity
floor: (a), (b) and (c) all measured green.

### The ask-again earned its keep three times over

The rule is to ask the panel once more AFTER the kill table is clean, capped at one
ask per detector per round. One ask, three escapes, all passing 31/31:

* **The seed collision.** `sq pr00 evt`/`sq d0 evt` assert that the guest's seed
  survives. Change the seed from `0x999` to `0x040` -- a plausible tidy-up -- and
  `sq miss evt` can no longer tell a raised 0x040 from a surviving seed, silently
  re-opening the payload-at-physical-zero escape. Fixed by an assertion rather than a
  convention: every SH-4 EXPEVT code is a multiple of 0x20, so the seed must not be.
  An enumerated list of codes would go stale the first time a row is added.
* **The SQMD guard.** A maintainer starting on `sh4sqwrite` writes
  `flags = (mmucr & SQMD) ? FLAG_WRITEFLAG : 0`. Every row left SQMD clear, so it
  passed all 31. `sq pr00 rdok` now sets it; the row is privileged, so SQMD cannot bar
  it, and the mutant reddens by judging PR=00 as a write.
* **The read-side protection code.** Corrupting `EXPEVT_TLB_PROT_LD` is invisible
  because every row is privileged and PR=00 permits a privileged read. FILED rather
  than fixed: it is a mutation in the general TLB table rather than in this call site,
  the detector is already above the vacuity floor, and a user-mode row carries a trap
  this project has already paid for once (the instruction fetch needs a user-accessible
  page, and an earlier witness measured a fetch fault instead of the access it meant).

### *** AND THE ASK-AGAIN FOUND A FOURTH, WHICH WAS A SHIPPED WRONG RECORD WITH WITNESSED CORRUPTION BEHIND IT ***

`gate_sh_rounding.sh` called `sq at0 qacr` *"the regression guard: with the MMU off the QACR
composition must be exactly as before."* **Measured false: the composition can be DELETED
OUTRIGHT and that row stays green.** It pins `addr & 0x03ffffe0` and nothing more.

Two structural reasons, neither of them bad luck. **No row in the probe had ever written
QACR0 or QACR1**, and `dev_sh4.c` seeds them nowhere, so `(((qacrN >> 2) & 7) << 26)` was
identically **zero** in every row — the term under test contributed nothing to any expected
value. And every SQ operand was `0xe00000e7`, bit 5 **set**, so `sq_nr` was 1 in all ten rows
and **QACR0 was never the register consulted, ever.**

The escape is **witnessed guest-visible corruption**, not a hypothesis: with AT=0 — the
ordinary store-queue mode, without paging — the destination area comes entirely from QACR, so
dropping the term or swapping the two registers lands 32 bytes on the wrong physical page.

**#454 made that edit more likely, which is why the rows ship with it.** This round adds three
comments saying that with the MMU on "QACR takes no part" and "the extaddr built above is
discarded"; a maintainer reading those and tidying the now-dead-looking composition four lines
above is exactly the six-months-later edit.

Three rows, measured: `sq qacr1 dst` (the area bits arrive), `sq qacr1 neg` (load-bearing —
without it a build writing to BOTH destinations passes), and `sq qacr0 sel`, which uses operand
`0xe00000c7` and is **the first row in the file to drive `sq_nr == 0` at all**, so it pins the
register selection and proves queue 0 is the source. Fixed build 34/34; composition deleted
31/34; `qacr0`/`qacr1` swapped 31/34.

Fixed in-round as L4 — prose claiming coverage a measurement refutes — rather than filed,
because the wrong record was live in the shipped tree. Several further escapes the same seat
measured are FILED rather than fixed: the two `itlb` rows carry no identity control (one
`dev_sh4.c` edit restores `FLAG_INSTR` to 31/31 and nothing reddens), user mode is entirely
unexercised, and the TEA/PTEH channel is unpinned.

### What the fix costs, stated rather than glossed

An SQ page now raises **the read-side faults only**: a TLB miss, and a protection
violation for a PR/privilege combination that forbids reading. What disappears is the
write-side pair -- the initial-page-write exception and write-side protection -- because
3.6.7 defines the former as occurring on "a data access (write)". Those two are exactly
what the STORE half owes, and this emulator does not judge the store half at all:
`sh_translate_v2p` maps `0xe0000000..0xe3ffffff` identically so an ordinary guest store
can reach the modelled queue SRAM. Measured, with liveness and device-signature controls
green: a store into the window succeeds against a PR=00 read-only entry and a clean one
alike. Filed as `sh4sqwrite`.

*An earlier draft of that paragraph said "an SQ page raises no MMU fault of any kind."
This round's own `sq miss evt` row disproves it, and a review seat caught it.*

One pass-1 seat dissented from the scope, holding that fixing the read half without the
write half is an unshippable intermediate state. Recorded by name rather than resolved
by majority: the round-scope rule decided it, and that seat's own proposed witness needs
a new oracle, which is the clause that excludes it.

### The record this corrects, dated on both ends

**2026-07-31 (#318, commit `6a2f41c`)** concluded *"It is a **write**, and the gate pins
it."* **2026-08-01 (commit `161641c`)** re-asserted it in a retrospective: *"re-reviewed
against the SH7750 manual and comes back **correct** ... the write classification is
load-bearing rather than cosmetic."*

**The "manual" in that sentence was not a manual.** No SH7750 document existed in this
tree until 2026-08-22. What was consulted was model recollection of one -- the same
citation class as #357/#362/#365. The first opening of the real 4.7.4 reversed it in one
sentence.

**The false premise, named because a wrong reason gets reused:** the argument assumed the
PREF flush is the only access ever judged against an SQ page's entry, so a bit consulted
only on writes had to be consumed by the flush. 4.7.4's first clause gives the write
judgement to the other access. The dirty-bit observation was true; the exclusivity under
it was invented.

**What held -- do not overcorrect.** Three of that retrospective's conclusions were later
CONFIRMED by the real manual and stand: translating the unmasked address and masking the
result (which is what preserves bits [9:5]); exception-XOR-store; and the withdrawal of
the false [25:6] bug entry. Only the classification failed -- and its follow-up inverted
with it: the *"regression that swapped the store-family event codes for load-family"* it
warned about was the fix, and `sq miss evt` now pins 0x040 where #318 required 0x060.

Corrected by this dated block plus pointers at the three sites. Live assertions -- source
comments, the gate, the probe -- are rewritten outright, because those are current claims
rather than history.

# GXemul 0.7.0 — `est/` Change Log

Authoritative record of every change made to the `est/` working copy while
hardening GXemul 0.7.0. Companion documents:

- **`CHANGES.patch`** — precise unified diff (original `src/` → `est/src/`). 56 source files (now incl. `devices/makeautodev.sh`). (Generated/build files — `*.o`, `tmp_*.c`, `auto*.c`, `Makefile`, `font8x*.c`, `ppc_spr_strings.h` — are excluded; the `-fgnu89-inline` `configure` fix is in both trees so it no longer diffs.)
- **`REVIEW_FINDINGS.md`** — full findings table, severities, and the fuzzing/validation methodology.
- **`../build/BUILD_NOTES.md`** — how to build (native WSL ext4; `-fgnu89-inline`).

**Status:** 67 corrections + 1 performance optimization (#67); extended by #69 (arc/jazz), #70–#88 (outstanding-bug remediation), and #89–#94 (multi-model review). **Primary gcc build: 0 errors / 0 warnings.** No ASan/UBSan
reports across the 6,772-case audit (cases run to timeout — no sanitizer signature observed,
*not* a full behavioral pass; the ASan/UBSan/clang/`-fanalyzer` configs emit pre-existing
non-fatal warnings, mostly in generated dyntrans code). Guests boot across **5 CPU arches**
(MIPS / PPC / SH4 / ARM / M88K) and **3 OS families** (NetBSD, OpenBSD, Linux).

> Source changes are confined to `est/src/**`. The `-fgnu89-inline` `configure` build
> fix is also applied to the root (baseline) `configure` so both trees build cleanly;
> the original `src/` *code* is untouched (kept as the orig-vs-est reference).

## #95 — central uninit-leak fix (Phase A) + #96–#100 (Phase B new-surface audit)
**#95 `cpus/memory_rw.c`** (root-cause): zero the caller's buffer on every device READ before the
len-clamp/dispatch, so a device handler that fills only part of `data` — or whose access is len-clamped —
can never return uninitialised host memory to the guest. Closes the whole class (cf. per-device #91/93/94).

| File | Corr. | What changed |
|------|-------|--------------|
| `devices/dev_kn01.c` | #96 | OB-8b: mask the overlay-palette *read* index `& 15` (16-entry array; the write index was masked in #75, read missed) — guest OOB palette read |
| `disk/bootblock_apple.c` | #97 | bound the partition loop (`ofs+0x40 <= sizeof(buf)`) + `%.32s` — `n_partitions=buf[0x207]` drove a ~130 KB OOB stack read on a malformed Apple-partition disk |
| `devices/dev_vga.c` | #98 | bound `vga_update_graphics` 8-bit/4-bit reads vs `gfx_mem_size` (OOB redraw read; complements #91) |
| `devices/dev_ps2_gs.c` | #99 | **CRITICAL**: reject `regnr (=relative_addr/16) >= N_GS_REGS` — guest 64-bit OOB heap **write** past `reg[264]` |
| `devices/dev_sgi_re.c` | #100 | `buf[4]`→`buf[8]` (bufdepth up to 8 stack overflow) + bound `tile_nr < 256` (re_tlb index) |

Phase B also ran a 3-agent fan-out (PROMs/framebuffers/disk-parsers): PROMs + config parser verified
CLEAN; 7 further agent candidates recorded in `OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md` (OB-27..33). scan-build clean.

## #130–#154 — full‑project multi‑model review + remediation
A whole‑codebase (not just recent‑changes) adversarial review of the core‑critical subset — the four CPU
instruction cores, the shared dynamic‑translation engine, the guest→host memory boundary + main loop, the
file loaders, network, disk, debugger, and the highest‑risk devices — explicitly weighing the original
author's *warn‑loudly / never‑silently‑mask / never‑crash‑on‑untrusted‑guest* ethos and the `doc/TODO.html`
wishlist. **Method:** parallel per‑subsystem Claude review agents → three independent cloud models
(GLM / DeepSeek‑V3 / Qwen3‑Coder) cross‑checking the top findings against the code → a Claude adjudicator
ruling every finding against the actual source and the pristine baseline. **~23 confirmed fixes; no false
positives survived; every confirmed bug is pre‑existing in the baseline** (the ~119‑item pass had not
reached them). The cores it *had* hardened — the dyntrans engine, the `memory_rw` boundary, and the
ELF/ECOFF/Mach‑O/a.out loaders — were re‑confirmed sound.

- **#137 (CRITICAL) — `cpus/cpu_mips_instr.c` `memset_addiu_bne_sw`.** `bytes_to_write = rY - rX` (unsigned)
  underflowed when a guest set *end < start*, and the page‑boundary clamp `(rX&0xfff)+bytes_to_write > 0x1000`
  itself wrapped mod 2^N → a **direct multi‑gigabyte `memset` into the host page** (bypassing the `memory_rw`
  clamp). Guest‑triggerable on pmax. **Fix:** fall back to the slow path when `rY < rX`.
- **#145 (HIGH) — `devices/dev_pvr.c`.** The framebuffer‑refresh copy was clamped to guest DIWSIZE geometry
  but not to the fixed 672×512 host framebuffer → guest→host heap **write**. **Fix:** also clamp to the host
  framebuffer's inner drawable area (proven bound).
- **#149 (HIGH) — `file/file_srec.c`.** A non‑hex byte survives (the loader warns but continues), so a record
  `count` reached 4335 against a 270‑byte buffer → ~4 KB host‑stack **over‑read** into guest RAM. **Fix:**
  clamp `count` to the actual parsed length (the parse loop is provably bounded).
- **Medium:** `#133` guest‑set SCSI `logical_block_size` overflow → OOM‑`exit(1)` (validate + 64‑bit math);
  `#130` TCP timestamp‑option over‑read echoed to the guest (length‑gate); `#141` PPC Time‑Base‑Upper never
  incremented (mask like DEC); `#146` five recoverable `dev_osiop` `exit(1)`s → warn‑once + stop the local
  engine; `#150` `free()` on an `mmap`‑backed `cpu` → `munmap`; `#136` uncapped boot‑image sizes → capped.
- **Low / hardening:** a `%s`‑with‑no‑argument trace format; two more small guest→host over‑reads (odd‑length
  ICMP checksum, short ARP); a NULL‑deref idle path; two missing nested‑delay‑slot guards; the inverted SH4
  store‑queue privilege test; SH FDIV‑by‑zero now yields the IEEE result; a debugger divide‑by‑zero guard;
  `strtoll`+range validation for numeric CLI options; a gzip temp‑file leak; residual signed‑shift UB casts;
  and a rate‑limited note on the device length‑clamp.

**Deferred (confirmed, but neither is a host‑safety issue and each fix's risk outweighs its low severity):**
a double‑precision op on an *odd* FP register (stays within the FP register union — not a host OOB), and the
nested‑delay‑slot guard being silent (already host‑safe; raising the architectural slot‑exception would be a
guest‑visible behaviour change across ~18 hot handlers).

**Verification:** build 0 errors / 0 warnings; a 9‑machine multi‑architecture boot sweep (all boot, no
regressions); the OpenBSD/pmax rig (full boot + root shell + NAT ping + clean halt); and a positive test
showing the S‑record loader now clamps the crafted over‑long record while a valid record still loads cleanly.

## Sixteenth round (#178–#181) — NE2000 / NAT hardening (Codex 5.6-Sol-Ultra NE2000 review, Fable-verified)
Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`/ultra reviewed the new arc NE2000 NIC (`src/devices/dev_ne2000.c`, 662 lines) plus its NAT and
Jazz-interrupt surface (report `../harness/codex_ne2000_to_fable.md`): 4 findings, **all confirmed REAL by a Fable
verifier (0 false positives), 0 CRITICAL** — the device's earlier panel fixes (RX FCS page-count, lost-interrupt
race, every card-memory access bounds-checked via `ne_mem_readb/writeb`) were re-confirmed sound.

| # | ID | Sev | File — fix |
|---|-----|-----|------------|
| **#178** | Cdx-NE.1 | **HIGH** | `net/net.c`+`net/net.h`, `devices/dev_ne2000.c`: unbounded NAT reply queue — a guest whose NE2000 receiver is disabled (`STP` / `RCR.MON`) enqueues replies that never drain → host OOM / `exit(1)`. **Fix:** per-`net` queued-packet counter + `NET_MAX_QUEUED_PACKETS` (256) drop-oldest cap; **and** the NE2000 drains its queue per-tick while stopped/monitor and makes CR `STP` dominate `STA` (rejects TXP while stopped) — closing both trigger variants. |
| **#179** | Cdx-NE.2 | MED | `devices/dev_jazz.c`: guest-reachable unconditional char-by-char `fatal()` on `R4030_SYS_CONFIG` / undefined offsets (host-output stall / log-fill DoS). **Fix:** ignore / return-0 + a once-only `debugmsg` (#119 idiom). |
| **#180** | Cdx-NE.3 | LOW | `devices/dev_ne2000.c`: `TPSR=0xff` TX source span aliases (16-bit wrap) into the station PROM, emitting card-private bytes as a valid frame. **Fix:** wide-arithmetic span check (`NE_RAM_START..NE_RAM_END`, `len ≤ NE_MAX_TX`) → set `TXE`, clear `TXP`, do not transmit. |
| **#181** | Cdx-NE.4 | LOW | `devices/dev_ne2000.c`: remote DMA kept accessing card RAM after `RBCR` reached 0 (a wide data-port access over-wrote past the count). **Fix:** early-out in `ne_dma_readb/writeb` when `rbcr==0` (no access, no `rsar++`; reads 0xff; RDC latch kept). |

Severity note: #180/#181 are hardware-fidelity / hardening — **no host OOB** (the aliased bytes are the
already-guest-readable PROM; the DMA over-write lands in RAM the guest already owns). **Build & regression:** builds
**0 errors / 0 warnings** (gcc 15.2.1, 2026-07-10); the rebuilt binary is the rigs' `gxsec-gxemul`; **both rigs
regression-pass** — pmax `le0` and arc NE2000 `ed0` each ping 0% loss + clean halt (the queue cap does not perturb
normal networking).

4-reviewer **Fable panel**, each finding source-verified by Fable. The panel had independently cleared the
memory-safety surface, so the headline is a **seam bug the area-partitioned panel missed and the holistic Codex pass
caught**: on a framebuffer *shrink*, `dev_fb_resize()` swaps the data pointer but leaves the device's registered
`length` stale, so the #155 dyntrans fast-map gate maps past the new, smaller allocation. This round fixes the
CRITICAL + the HIGH + the clean part of the guest-`exit(1)` cluster; the render-loop `exit(1)`s and the remaining
Codex medium/lows are triaged in `OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md`.

| # | ID | Sev | File — fix |
|---|-----|-----|------------|
| **#182** | Cdx.1 | **CRITICAL** | `core/memory.c`+`include/memory.h`, `devices/dev_fb.c`: `dev_fb_resize()` called `memory_device_update_data()` (swaps only the dyntrans data pointer) but never shrank the device's registered `length`; the #155 fast-map gate `(paddr|mask) < length` then trusted the OLD length and installed a writable host mapping past the end of the new, smaller framebuffer → guest-controlled OOB host write (e.g. SGI O2/GBE `HCMAP` shrink 1280→640, then touch offset 0x200000). Latent in pristine upstream. **Fix:** new `memory_device_update_length()` keeps `length`/`endaddr`/`mmap_dev_maxaddr` in sync on resize; the existing #157 cache-invalidate then drops stale fast-path pointers. |
| **#183** | Cdx.2 | **HIGH** | `console/x11.c`: `x11_fb_resize()` computed the XImage allocation `new_xsize*new_ysize*alloc_depth/8` in 32-bit `int`; a guest-reachable resize within #156's 16384/axis cap (e.g. 12000×12000×32bpp) overflows `int`, under-allocates, then `XPutPixel` overruns the buffer → out-of-bounds host write on X11 builds. **Fix:** widen the arithmetic to `size_t`. |
| **#184** | Cdx.4 | MED | `devices/dev_fb.c`: the `dev_fb_resize()` too-small (`<10`) branch still did `exit(1)`; guest-reachable via GBE `HCMAP`/`VCMAP` written with a tiny/zero dimension → emulator-abort DoS. **Fix:** reject and keep the old framebuffer (return), matching the sibling `>16384` branch (#156 idiom). |
| **#186** | Cdx.6 | MED | `devices/dev_mb89352.c`: a valid guest `SCMD_XFR` with an unimplemented `PCTL` phase (4/5/6) hit `exit(1)`. **Fix:** log + `break` (#119 idiom). |
| **#187** | Cdx.7 | MED | `devices/dev_pvr.c`: eight guest-reachable PVR **MMIO register-write** `exit(1)`s (STARTRENDER read; OB_ADDR / TILEBUF_ADDR / TA_OPB_START / TA_OB_START unknown-bit; DIWCONF magic; TA access-len; and the default unhandled-register case). **Fix:** log-and-continue (mask-and-`DEFAULT_WRITE` / `break`), matching #166/#176. |

Provenance/severity: **#182 CRITICAL** overturns the Fable-panel-only "memory-safety clean" read — a genuine
out-of-bounds framebuffer write, latent in pristine upstream, exposed by any framebuffer that shrinks (SGI GBE, or
`fbctrl`). **#183 HIGH** is X11-build-only. #184/#186/#187 are availability (`exit(1)`) DoS, converted per the fork's
#118/#119 log-and-continue ethos. **Deferred (documented in `OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md`, not silently dropped):** the ASC
`data_out_len==0` `exit(1)` (#185 — needs a structural transfer-skip), the four PVR render/texture-loop `exit(1)`s

overlay silent-fail, Jazz LB_IE / dual-pending IRQ, ARC partition signed-`*512`, TCP-debug over-read, NE2000 TX
