The FPSCR is eight **four**-bit fields and the FM field has one bit per field, so
the decoder builds the write mask a nibble at a time. It shifted by **eight** bits
per iteration while ORing in four:

```c
	for (bi=7; bi>=0; bi--) {
		ic->arg[1] <<= 8;
		if (iword & (1 << (17+bi)))
			ic->arg[1] |= 0xf;
	}
```

so the mask sprawled across sixty-four bits. The first four FM bits landed entirely
above the 32-bit FPSCR and wrote **nothing**; the rest wrote the wrong fields.
Measured with every field selected and a source of all ones, the register came back
`0x0f0f0f0f` instead of `0xffffffff`; `FM=0x80` wrote nothing at all; and `FM=0x01`
was correct only by the coincidence of being the final iteration, with no shift
after it. One character: the stride is 4.

This is why gate 13 sets FPSCR by **debugger write** everywhere rather than through
the guest's own `mtfsf`, and why its mode rows read FPSCR back afterwards: a mode
that silently failed to take would have turned every directed-mode row into a second
copy of the RN row. That precaution is what made this finding possible — had the
gate driven the mode through `mtfsf`, the defect would have been baked into the
measurement instead of exposed by it. The debugger write stays for exactly that
reason, and `mtfsf` now has six rows of its own.

### #325 — fctiwz converted a NaN to zero

The ISA gives a NaN the same answer as an operand below the representable range:
the most negative value. This returned **zero**, which is the worse kind of wrong —
a legitimate result the guest cannot distinguish from a successful conversion of
0.0. Two lines.

### The part worth reading: the row that recorded that divergence never measured it

`fctiwz`'s defect has been pinned in gate 13 as a known divergence since #304, with
its committed answer recorded as `00000000`. **That row was not measuring `fctiwz`
of a NaN.** Its instruction word was `0xFC00001E`, whose frB field is **zero**, so
it converted `f0` while the probe seeded the operand into `f1`. The answer was zero
because it converted an empty register.

The source reading behind the original filing was right, and the row that appeared
to confirm it was measuring something else that happened to agree. Two independent
wrongs producing one plausible number is exactly the failure this harness exists to
prevent, and it survived a round-69 five-seat review and every run since.

It was caught only because the fix did not change the row. Chasing that produced
the diagnostic that mattered: **`fctiwz` of 1.0 also returned zero**, which no
theory of the NaN path can explain.

Two things follow, and both are in the gate now:

- The scope is exactly one encoding. Every other hand-assembled word in that probe
  was decoded field by field and is correct — `FRSP_F0_F1` genuinely has frB=1, so
  #304's verification, which is most of this gate, stands.
- The new **`fctiwz 1.0 control`** row is the one that could have caught it from the
  start. With a wrong frB the answer is zero for *any* operand, and every existing
  `fctiwz` row expected `0x80000000` or `0` — values a broken encoding can produce
  by accident. A row whose expected answer is small and nonzero cannot.

That is the third time in this project a hand-assembled encoding has nearly
manufactured a finding, and the first time one reached a committed gate.

### The after-pass: two seats disagreed about the ISA, and the ISA answered

The five-seat review of the finished diff split on one question — what `fctiwz` owes
for an operand that is too *large and positive*, a branch neither correction touches.
One seat held that PowerPC saturates to `0x7fffffff`. Another held that PowerPC uses a
single invalid sentinel, `0x80000000`, for every bad operand the way x87 does, and
filed the unchanged branch as a defect the round should have fixed.

Settled from Book I rather than by counting seats. The instruction's own definition:

> If the operand in FRB is greater than 2^31 - 1, then bits 32:63 of FRT are set to
> `0x7FFF_FFFF`. If the operand in FRB is less than -2^31, then bits 32:63 of FRT are
> set to `0x8000_0000`.

and Appendix A.2's model splits the invalid cases three ways: **Infinity Operand** and
**Large Operand** both branch on sign, while **SNaN Operand** and **QNaN Operand**
return `0x8000_0000` unconditionally. So the existing branch is right, the proposed
change would have been a regression, and #325's unconditional `0x80000000` for NaN is
right for both NaN kinds and both signs.

One thing had to be checked before that conclusion held, because #325 could have
broken infinities by accident: `ieee_interpret_float_value` does **not** set `nan` for
±Inf — it takes the `zero_or_no_reasonable_result` path, which applies the sign — so
`frb.nan` is false for infinities and they still reach the sign-dependent branches.
Had that function classified Inf as NaN, #325 would have turned `fctiwz(+Inf)` from
`0x7fffffff` into `0x80000000`.

The disagreement was worth having: it landed on a branch with **no gate coverage at
all**. Four rows now pin it — `+Inf`, `-Inf`, `2^31`, `-(2^31+1)` — so the misreading
that was proposed here cannot be applied later without a gate going red.

### What the same pass found in the gate rows themselves

Three more, each from a different seat and each verified before being acted on:

**The `mtfsf FM=0x80` row blesses a defect.** Field 0 is FX, FEX, VX, OX, and Book I's
own note says FX and OX come from `(FRB)32` and `(FRB)35` while *"Bits 1 and 2 (FEX and
VX) are set according to the usual rule ... and not from (FRB)33:34"* — they are OR
summaries and `mtfsf` must never copy them. This emulator copies all four, so it answers
`f0000000` where hardware answers `90000000`. Two seats found this independently. The row
stays, because it is what measures #324's field placement, but it is now labelled as
recording a divergence rather than conformance, and **`FM=0x40` was added as the clean
companion**: field 1 carries no summary bits.

That companion turned out to be the row worth having for another reason. Field 1 holds
**VXSNAN** — the sticky bit #304 made the emulator set, and which `frsp`'s own comment
names `mtfsf` as the guest's way to clear. Under the old stride, field 1's nibble landed
at bits 48–51, above the 32-bit FPSCR. **The guest could not clear VXSNAN at all.** #324
is what makes that documented path real; nobody had connected the two defects.

**Every `mtfsf` row measured only half the handler.** All of them started from a zeroed
FPSCR and wrote ones, so `fpscr &= ~mask` could have been deleted entirely and all four
would still have passed. One row now preloads all ones and writes zeros into the selected
field, so the clearing half is measured too.

**`fctiwz 1.0` cannot pin round-toward-zero.** An integer converts identically under
every rounding mode, so a decode that reached `fctiw` (XO 14, rounds per RN) instead of
`fctiwz` (XO 15) would pass it. `1.9 → 1` and `-1.9 → -1` separate them; nearest would
give 2 and -2. The control row was doing the job it was added for — proving the operand
register is read — and none of the job its name implied.

One caveat is recorded rather than acted on: the `>= 2147483647.0` / `<= -2147483648.0`
comparisons give the right *result* for every operand, but they are not a correct
*classification* of which operands are out of range. The model range-checks after
rounding, so under round-toward-zero an operand stays convertible while
`x < 2147483648.0`. Anyone who later reuses these branches to raise VXCVI will flag
exact endpoints and the fractional fringe that are not invalid at all.

### Still open in this cluster, deliberately

`fmuls`, `fadds`, `fsubs` and `fdivs` are bare aliases of their double-precision
handlers, each with a `/* TODO */` — they do not narrow at all. That is not a
one-liner: doing it properly means computing in double, rounding once to single
under FPSCR's mode, and representing the result back in double, which is #308's
round-to-odd machinery plus rounding-mode plumbing this round did not build. The
exception-enable bits (OE/UE/VE) and the FPRF class field remain unmodelled, and
the splice-letter divergence at ~2^129 stays a deliberate policy pin.

## Retrospective review of round 81 (#318) — the code stands, one bug record did not

> **[2026-08-22, #454: the write-type conclusion below is REVERSED by the real 4.7.4 -- see the Round 454 block at the top of this file. The address-composition, exception-XOR-store and [25:6] conclusions stand.]**

Part of the standing rule that shipped work gets a panel pass after the fact, not only
before. #318 (the SH-4 store-queue flush with the MMU on) was re-reviewed against the
SH7750 manual and comes back **correct**: the exception-XOR-store property holds (a
failing translation returns before the copy loop, and every failing path inside
`translate_via_mmu` raises through the `exception:` label), the store-family EXPEVT/TEA/
PTEH/SPC state is right for the guest to fault and retry, translating the *unmasked*
address and masking the *result* is what preserves bits [9:5] as the manual requires, and
the write classification is load-bearing rather than cosmetic — a read classification
would let a flush to a clean page skip `EXPEVT_TLB_MOD` and lose the dirty bit, which is
exactly what gate 10's `sq at1 clean` row pins.

**What did not survive is an entry in `OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md`.** It claimed the store-queue
identity mapping ignores address bits [25:6], "so a guest filling a queue through a
non-zero offset stores where the flush will not read it". That is false. `memory_sh.c:301`
passes the **full** virtual address through, and the store-queue device wraps its index
with `% sizeof(d->sq)` (`dev_sh4.c:952`), so bits [5:0] — the queue select and the offset
within it — survive intact and an aliased fill lands exactly where the flush reads. That
is hardware's own don't-care treatment of [25:6], not a defect.

It was a bug report filed against correct behaviour, and it had been sitting in the queue
as scheduled work. Corrected in the record and withdrawn from round 82's task, with the
reason kept: a false entry in a bug list is not free — it costs a future round the time to
re-derive it, and it is the same dishonest-listing class #270 exists to prevent. The
review also noted a genuine gap the round did not have: gate 10's store-queue rows assert
the memory effect but pin none of the exception registers, so a regression that swapped
the store-family event codes for load-family would pass everything except one row. Folded
into round 82, which is already building the user-mode witness those rows need.

## Not changed (assessed, intentionally left)
- ELF64 `st_name` "truncation" — **false positive**: gxemul's `exec_elf.h` defines
  `Elf64_Half = uint32_t` (32-bit), so it is not truncated.
- Signed `byte<<24` assembly in the **CPU instruction cores** (e.g. `cpu_arm_instr_loadstore.c`,
  found via the per-device runtime fuzz) — UBSan-only, deterministic, hottest code path. The
  shared file-decoder source (`unencode`) is now fixed (#27); the per-arch instruction load/store
  assembly is left (whack-a-mole across every core, no real bug).
- a.out timeout signature — the emulator *running* a loaded garbage program until timeout
  (expected behaviour, not a loader bug).

### The last thing a gate caught was a citation that decayed by MULTIPLYING

Section X failed the round on four BARE artifact names -- `probe_Mb.raw`, `probe_Md1.raw`,
`probe_Md2.raw`, `probe_Mnull.raw` -- each with **seven candidates**. Every one was
unambiguous when written, because there was one table. Five tables later the same string
names seven different measurements and picks none.

**That is the citation-decay class arriving from a direction the round had not seen.** It had
already been bitten by citations going stale because the FILE moved under them, five times.
This one went stale because the NAMESPACE filled up underneath it -- the text never changed
and stopped being true anyway.

*The fix is the same one the rule already demands and this round applied everywhere else: a
measurement cited in a durable record lives at a durable, QUALIFIED path.*

### Three pre-commit obligations, discharged and named

An adjudication named three things owed before the commit. All three were done; naming them
because *"if not, they are now record gaps for the next records audit to find, and it will."*

* **A SECOND READING of the round's own corrections.** *"A correction is not safer than the thing
  it corrects"* has four measured instances here. The re-read found a fifth: the `debug()`
  citation, already corrected once from `:200,:203` to `:231,:234`, had gone stale AGAIN when the
  comment was trimmed three lines shorter, and is now `:228,:231`. **A correction that goes stale
  a second time is the strongest case for the rule.**
* **The un-fired seat's disposition.** Opus 5 was not fired on pass 2 — deliberately reserved —
  and was then fired as the single capped ask-again, where it produced the `+1` translation
  escape. The gap closed by the seat being used, not by the record explaining its absence.
* **The install-time list diff.** The gate section was installed and then EVERY `for v in` list in
  `gate_sh_rounding.sh` was diffed against the pre-install file: **11 lists became 12, and the
  only change was the new `$ASLOG` block.** That check exists because a first-match regex once
  wrote one section's row names over another's, and the verification that shared the regex passed
  on it. `bash -n` clean, and every other section's `count "$XXLOG"` discriminator untouched.

### And the correction that reported five mis-counts contained a sixth

The scope correction for `ledgerstatelies` reported **11 rows** while its own class column summed
to **13**. Both are right and I never showed the arithmetic:

> 13 instances − 1 dedup (`fbwitness` is in two classes: closed-no-witness AND closed-no-commits)
> − 1 self (`ledgerstatelies` is the tracking row for the repair itself) = **11 rows to repair**

An adjudicating seat refused to let either number be quoted until the reconciliation existed.
*That is the second-reading rule applied to a correction about counting errors — and it was
right to.*

### *** THE LARGEST STATEMENT OF WHAT THIS ROUND ACTUALLY FIXED, ARRIVED LAST ***

The round measured the kill as reachable at **64 byte addresses** by a probe census. The assess
stage, filled after the commit, found TRANSACTION CLOSURE — and its consequence is bigger than a
count:

> **A CPU-VALID INSTRUCTION AIMED AT A DOCUMENTED REGISTER, BUT USING THE WRONG DEVICE ACCESS
> WIDTH, REACHES THE KILL.**
>
> *The width clause is not decoration and an earlier draft of this box dropped it. Without it
> the sentence reads as a universal, and the universal is FALSE: no 32-bit access to any of the
> twelve implemented registers kills — all twelve labels give r <= 2.*

An 8-byte `fmov.d` is 8-byte aligned, so its base is a **word-0 or word-2** offset. Based at one
of the four **word-2** registers (+0x08, +0x18, +0x28, +0x38) it touches words 2 and 3, and word
3 is a killing lane — so the instruction never has to name a reserved address to reach one.

**The count is FOUR, not "every documented register", and the difference is checkable:** based
at a word-0 register (+0x00, +0x10, +0x20, +0x30) an `fmov.d` touches words 0 and 1 and does NOT
die; word-1 registers (+0x04 and siblings) are not 8-byte aligned, so they cannot be an `fmov.d`
base at all. *A packet-fed seat refused to sign the "every"-shaped entailment and asked for it
to be settled from source rather than from the arithmetic. It settles: the set is the four
word-2 registers.*

That enlarges the severity in KIND, not in count: this was not only "a guest that walks reserved
space can end the host", it was "a guest aiming at a register it is entitled to use can end the
host, without ever naming a reserved address."

#### *** THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS BLOCK SAID "LEGAL", "ordinary, correct guest code", "Normal
#### driver traffic" AND "uses the device correctly". ALL FOUR ARE WITHDRAWN — pass 2 on this
#### commit refuted them, and the refutation came with an external oracle. ***

*** AND THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS WITHDRAWAL COMMITTED THE ERROR IT WAS WITHDRAWING. ***
It asserted, bolded, **"The Holly ASIC's documented access width is 32-bit"** — while this
round's own commit message says *"This project holds no Holly ASIC documentation."* What was
actually supplied is **two DRIVER IMPLEMENTATIONS**: Linux's `mach-dreamcast` IRQ model and
KallistiOS, both using `inl`/`outl`, i.e. 32-bit accesses to three status words and three per
mask group. **A driver's access width is strong implementation evidence; it is not a documented
width**, and collapsing the two is this project's own evidence ladder (CONFIRMED versus
BELIEVED) failing inside the paragraph that withdraws four unsupported words.

**The withdrawal survives without that warrant, which is why the conclusion stands.** It was
re-derived independently and mechanically from the file's own twelve `case` labels: every one
gives r <= 2, so **no 32-bit access to any implemented register kills**. "Legal", "correct" and
"normal driver traffic" were unsupported on the source alone, with no external oracle needed.
An 8-byte `fmov.d` is CPU-valid but is not a 32-bit device access, and it necessarily includes
a reserved address.

*The rule that failed here is the PREMISE-AUDIT one — state a load-bearing premise as a
question. An earlier draft blamed the WARRANT-ELEMENTS rule, which governs TRANSFERRING A
PRECEDENT; this claim transferred nothing, it was a severity claim. Citing the wrong rule is how
a carrier accretes rules nobody can test.*

*This is the WARRANT-ELEMENTS rule failing on the round that minted it. The rule says: before
transferring a precedent, grep the round's own findings against each element. The element never
checked was the DEVICE's access width, and no amount of checking register adjacency or decoder
splitting could substitute for it.*

**Three further corrections in the same block, each from a different seat:**

* **The store-queue flush SPANS two killing words and DIES ON THE FIRST.** It does not "hit two".
  The burst commits +0x00, +0x04 and +0x08, then exits the host at +0x0c and never reaches the
  second. "Dying mid-burst with earlier words already committed" is right for the SQ case and
  WRONG for the `fmov.d` case, where the killing word is issued first and nothing commits.
* **The `fmov.d` issue-order claim is OVER-GENERAL and is not load-bearing.** `cpu_sh_instr.c:790-798`
  covers only `fmov_rm_frn`'s SZ=1 path; **three of the six SZ=1 encodings are low-word first**
  (`fmov @Rm+,DRn` and `fmov @(R0,Rm),DRn` among them). The host dies either way — whichever half
  lands on +0x0c — so the ORDER was never needed. It was cited as a warrant anyway.
  *A seat had already recorded this on the `#463` pass 2, in the receipt for `f1fa6a0`, and it
  was cited again here without being consulted.*
* **"64 is a floor" was ambiguous between two different sets, and the two seats that argued about
  it were counting different things.** Stated exactly: there are **64 killing BYTE ADDRESSES**
  (four bytes of word 3 × sixteen groups), and that set is complete, not a floor. What is a floor
  is the set of **transaction STARTS that end in death**, which additionally contains the sixteen
  8-byte bases (+0x08, +0x18 … +0xf8) and the eight aligned 32-byte store-queue blocks — none of
  which is itself one of the 64.

### And a wording pass the round owes, because it asserted C where it had only a measurement

Throughout, this round wrote **`mask_13[4]` IS `mask_11[1]`** as a fact. It is not a fact of C —
it is a *toolchain-measured aliasing outcome*, and the subscript is **undefined behaviour**
regardless of member adjacency. Every seat, the adjudicator and I treated it as defined layout
all round.

The correction cuts TOWARD the fix rather than against it: the failure a broken invariant buys is
not a defined overlap but UB a compiler is licensed to exploit, which is a stronger argument for
enforcing the bound in control flow than any of the ones actually made. Corollary, said out loud
because it was true of the tables anyway: **mutants whose kills route through an out-of-bounds
subscript are toolchain-measured oracles**, not portable ones — and there are **FIVE of them, not
the two an earlier draft named**: `-1`, the array shrink `[3]`->`[2]`, `& 7` (max r = 6), and
BOTH translations `+1` and `+2`. `& 2`, `& 1`, `/ 2` and `% 3` all keep r <= 2 and are not in
the class. *Evidence for `& 7`: `table3_12rows/probe_M7.raw` shows `crossarr` reading **0xd4** where base
reads **0xc3** — an out-of-bounds neighbour value, layout-dependent. **The two omissions that
matter most are `+1` and `+2`, and nobody named them until now:** `+1` is `mask9 rt`'s own
mutant — the thirteenth row, the anchored accept row, and the exemplar carrier clause (f) was
minted from — while `+2` is the measured anchor cited in the `asicindexcase` warrant. None of
this changes a shipped row; it changes what the probe's CONTRACT may claim under floor clause
(e), because three of the detector's five aliasing kills are toolchain-measured rather than
portable. That belongs in the probe header.*

### The latch: considered, and refuted BY THIS ROUND'S OWN EARLIER FINDING

An in-tree precedent (a bounded diagnostic in the memory dispatcher) suggested replacing the
deleted `fatal()` with a latched one. It was ruled in, and then refuted:

* **The predicate is empty where it matters** — "latch only on offsets that are not a lane of a
  legal multi-word access" selects the empty set inside the modelled groups.
* **The information is absent, not merely awkward** — the decoder issues two independent 32-bit
  accesses (this round's own finding 7, *"read second word first"*), so at the handler the second
  half of a legal `fmov.d` and a direct probe of a reserved word are **byte-identical calls**.

#### *** BOTH BULLETS ARE TRUE ONLY FOR `len == 4`, AND AS WRITTEN THEY OVERCLAIM. Corrected in
#### the pass 2 on this commit, by THREE seats independently — two file-reading, one packet-fed. ***

The handler receives `len` as well as `relative_addr`. So:

* a **byte** access at +0x0d, or a **word** access at +0x0e, is not a lane of any legal 8-byte
  access, and is distinguishable by `len` alone;
* an **unaligned** call is distinguishable by `relative_addr` alone.

A predicate like **"not an aligned 4-byte subaccess"** is therefore *demonstrably nonempty*, and
a bounded diagnostic on it would announce nothing a legal `fmov.d` or store-queue burst produces.
**What the two bullets actually establish is narrower: an aligned 32-bit access at +0x0c cannot
be told from the half of an `fmov.d`, so a latch cannot cover THAT case without false alarms.**

*And the second bullet leans on the issue-order claim, which is over-general — see the correction
above. Since the host dies on whichever half lands at +0x0c, indistinguishability never needed
the order, and citing it made the argument look better-warranted than it was.*

**PROVENANCE, corrected — an earlier draft of this very block got it wrong.** That draft said a
seat had recorded the over-generality "in the receipt for `f1fa6a0`". **The receipt mentions
`fmov` zero times.** What actually happened is worse and is a class this project already names:
grok DID record it, in its seat answer on the earlier pass-2 panel
(`_scratchpad/panel_20260825_020219/grok.txt`), naming `fmov @Rm+,DRn` at `:943-963` and
`fmov @(R0,Rm),DRn` at `:866-890` as low-word-first — **and it was never transcribed into the
receipt.** So the next round could not consult it. *That is the UNREAD REVIEW class: a seat that
answered and was not recorded is neither a seat failure nor agreement. Third recorded instance,
and the first where the unread finding was then independently re-derived a round later.*

**DISPOSITION, and it is deliberately not a reversal.** Silent fall-through remains defensible as
POLICY — declining to announce a class you can only partially discriminate is a real design
choice. What this round may **not** claim is that it was FORCED: the commit said the option was
refuted, and it was not. This is a DESIGN DISSENT against a record, not a measured false pass, so
the code is unchanged and the record is corrected. The filed follow-up (`asicindexcase`) inherits
a genuinely open question rather than a closed one.

*Note what this does to the sentence below.* The warrant-elements rule was minted from the claim
that "the defeating fact was already in the record". The fact was there; it just did not defeat
as much as was claimed. **The rule survives its own founding example being weaker than stated** —
which is worth recording, because a rule whose exemplar quietly erodes is how a carrier
accumulates confident text nobody re-checks.

*The defeating fact was already in this round's record, filed under a different heading.* The
transfer test checked whether the precedent's "common and benign" element carried — it did not —
while the vulnerable element was "announces something REAL", and finding 7 had already answered
it. **Before transferring a precedent, grep the round's own findings against each warrant
element.**
